To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the new notions of completeness and soundness are useful for evaluating saliency methods; 2) they allow a new and stronger justification for the use of several tricks in the field, such as T.V. regularization, and upscaling; and 3) these notions are also useful in other fields, such as the evaluation of the explanations of the predictions of a trained classifier.

(i) a saliency method can be {\em sound} (and thus, useful for explaining the net's output) even if it does not satisfy the completeness criterion, and (ii) the heuristic tricks of T.V. regularization, and upscaling are useful for making saliency methods sound.

(1) The most common saliency methods are not sound, i.e. they may fail to explain a net's output even when the input is a certificate for that output, (2) The most common methods are also incomplete, i.e. their explanations may not be the best possible explanations, and (3) The most common tricks in the field, such as T.V. regularization and upscaling, are justified by soundness, not completeness.
